question.title: Consecutive Logins
question.desc: Find the users with the most consecutive days of logging in, along with the start and end dates of their longest streak.
question.setup: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users; CREATE TABLE users (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(255)); DROP TABLE IF EXISTS logins; CREATE TABLE logins (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, user_id INTEGER, login_date DATE); INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Alice'), ('Bob'), ('Charlie'); INSERT INTO logins (user_id, login_date) VALUES (1, '2022-01-01'), (1, '2022-01-02'), (1, '2022-01-03'), (2, '2022-01-01'), (2, '2022-01-03'), (3, '2022-01-01'), (3, '2022-01-02'), (3, '2022-01-03'), (3, '2022-01-04');
question.solution: WITH ranked_logins AS ( SELECT user_id, login_date, DATEADD('day', -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date), login_date) AS group_date FROM logins ), streaks AS ( SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS start_date, MAX(login_date) AS end_date, COUNT(*) AS streak FROM ranked_logins GROUP BY user_id, group_date ) SELECT u.name, s.start_date, s.end_date, s.streak FROM streaks s JOIN users u ON s.user_id = u.id ORDER BY s.streak DESC LIMIT 2;
question.tips: Consider using window functions to identify consecutive sequences.
hints: Use a Common Table Expression (CTE) to simplify the query and improve readability.
You will need to use the ROW_NUMBER() function to assign a unique number to each row within each partition of the result set.
The DATEADD function can be used to calculate the group date by subtracting the row number from the login date.
